title: The Lucena Position
subtitle: Building a bridge to shelter the king
summary: The Lucena position is the single most important rook-endgame technique: with the pawn one square from queening and the king already in front of it, White builds a 'bridge' with the rook to shield the king from checks and force promotion.

rootAnnotations.title: What makes this a Lucena position
rootAnnotations.body: White's king already stands on the queening square, the pawn is one step from promoting, and Black's king is cut off on the far side of the board — it can never approach to help. Black's only resource is checking with the rook from behind. This exact skeleton, with a non-rook-pawn, is always a win if White knows the technique.

rootAnnotations.title: The problem to solve
rootAnnotations.body: White's king must step aside so the pawn can promote, but every square it tries leads to a check along a rank from Black's rook — and each further check would push the king away from the pawn. 'Building the bridge' means placing White's own rook on the fourth rank so it can block those checks the instant they come.

annotations.title: Step one: chase the king off the back rank
annotations.body: Before building the bridge, White uses the rook to push Black's king away from d8, buying room to maneuver. This check forces the king to a square where it can no longer interfere.

annotations.title: Forced retreat
annotations.body: The king has to give ground; d8 and the d-file are no longer available.

annotations.title: Interposing loses the rook outright
annotations.body: Blocking with the rook instead of moving the king is a serious mistake — the rook on d2 is completely undefended, and White simply captures it.

annotations.title: Game over
annotations.body: White is now a full rook ahead with a pawn one step from queening — a trivial win. This is why Black must retreat the king instead of interposing.

annotations.title: Building the bridge
annotations.body: This is the move that gives the whole technique its name. The rook takes up a post on the fourth rank, exactly far enough from the eventual checking squares to block them the moment they're needed — like a bridge the king will walk across to safety.

annotations.title: Repositioning to keep checking
annotations.body: Black's rook returns to the a-file, the only file from which it can still harass White's king as it comes forward.

annotations.title: The king finally steps aside
annotations.body: With the rook ready on the fourth rank, White's king can leave the queening square without fear — any rank check can now be blocked.

annotations.title: Black keeps checking — the only try
annotations.body: Checking from behind is Black's sole practical resource. Each check will simply push the White king one step closer to the bridge.

annotations.title: Checks are running out of room
annotations.body: Black keeps checking from the side the White king isn't shielded from, but the king is steadily closing the distance to the rook on d4.

annotations.title: One check left
annotations.body: The White king has reached the fourth rank right next to its own rook — exactly the moment the bridge was built for.

annotations.title: The bridge is complete
annotations.body: The rook interposes on b4, blocking the check while staying protected by the king. Black's rook can no longer give a useful check without simply being captured — Rxb4+ Kxb4 trades down to a king-and-pawn endgame that is an elementary win, and any other rook move lets the b-pawn queen immediately.
